A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ReVISE work. Their complete main texts and Appendices A–C, including equations, tables and figures, support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original GSM8K and MATH-500 experiments, curriculum and loss ablations, sampling analyses, and iterative-refinement results.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds coding, transfer, baseline-comparison, iterative-training and extended-sampling results.

M1.justification: Appendix B.2 adds an iterative-training variant that resamples reasoning-path pairs from the current model and repeats preference optimization. The core two-stage training, losses, verification tokens and confidence-aware decoding remain unchanged. Iterative refinement during inference already appeared in v1.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual training and evaluation on MBPP Python programming problems, extending the demonstrated coverage beyond mathematics. It also introduces a distinct transfer scenario: training on MATH and evaluating on GSM8K (Table 4). These experiments were absent from v1, despite its introductory reference to coding.

E2.justification: v2 adds standalone DPO comparisons on GSM8K and MATH-500 (Table 5), a SCoRe comparison on Gemma-2-2B (Table 6), and comparison with the V-STaR verifier (Table 7). The SCoRe scores explicitly come from its original paper. Standalone DPO is distinct from v1’s existing ablation removing DPO loss.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce MBPP Pass@1 and three-shot prompting with supplied tests, Gemma-2-2B experiments, and Llama-3.1-8B evaluation on GSM8K. Appendix B extends sampling budgets from at most eight to 64 generations and evaluates additional training cycles with generation-budget comparisons. These are added protocols; the established mathematics training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of cross-dataset transfer, performance across repeated training cycles, and verifier discrimination relative to V-STaR, while extending sampling-budget sensitivity through 64 generations. Existing curriculum/loss ablations and qualitative examples are retained. Figure 8’s iterative-inference analysis moves from Appendix B.1 into Section 4.3 and is not new.

E5.justification: Unlike v1’s point estimates, v2 Table 8 reports ± quantities for the extended scaling results, such as 37.7% ± 0.5 at Maj@64. Their statistical meaning, run counts and seeds are unspecified, so this establishes additional uncertainty reporting but not an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: Shared Table 1 Maj@1/Maj@5 values remain unchanged, while substantial new results cover coding, transfer, additional model configurations and comparators. Examples include MBPP Pass@1 of 33.1% versus STaR+’s 30.7% (Table 2), Gemma accuracies of 23.2%, 24.2% and 25.8% across training cycles (Table 6), and 37.7% ± 0.5 at Maj@64 (Table 8). These are added evaluations, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: The mathematical setup, preference-pair definitions, training losses and confidence-weighted aggregation rule in Section 3 are unchanged. Neither version supplies additional theoretical propositions or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about intrinsic verification, self-correction, two-stage preference training and efficient test-time scaling. Mathematical and coding applicability was already claimed in v1; the new coding experiment supplies evidence for that retained claim.

C2.justification: New discussion interprets transfer results as evidence of domain generalization and repeated-training results as demonstrating practical scalability. Appendix B.2 adds a claimed 30-fold training-cost advantage over SCoRe based on generation counts and acknowledges using published SCoRe results because code was unavailable. Existing mechanism explanations and limitations remain largely unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-availability link, MBPP data-construction details specifying 16 valid GPT-4o reasoning/code paths per problem, and its prompt template and three demonstrations. Appendix B also documents DPO pair construction and generation counts for the new training comparison. Existing optimizer, hyperparameter and hardware disclosures are retained; most mathematics prompt material is reorganized.

R1.justification: Austin et al. (2021) is newly cited for MBPP. Appendix B develops more explicit competitive positioning against already-cited DPO, SCoRe and V-STaR, particularly concerning training efficiency and intrinsic verification. The substantive related-work review otherwise remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. v2 moves the iterative-inference discussion into Section 4.3, reorganizes Appendix B and the prompt documentation, removes a short related-work preamble, and adds acknowledgements, correspondence information and proceedings text. This is localized reorganization rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: Table 1 is restructured to include 8B GSM8K results and omit its Maj@3 columns, and six new experimental tables are added. Figure 8 is relocated and resized. Appendix examples become captioned tables with integrated, colored verification tokens, while prompts are redesigned into separate template and demonstration tables. Existing plots retain their underlying results.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support: MBPP directly addresses v1’s unsupported coding claim, transfer testing probes generalization beyond the training dataset, and DPO/V-STaR comparisons better test the proposed training and intrinsic verification. Extended sampling and iterative-training experiments further substantiate scalability. These gains outweigh remaining reporting weaknesses, including undefined ± quantities, a DPO table/prose discrepancy, and SCoRe efficiency claims based on published scores and generation counts rather than matched runtime measurements.
